passage:
Sofia: Found the perfect dress for Ana's wedding! $280 though.
Jules: Ouch.
Sofia: Here's the thing: Marlowe's lets you return anything within 30 days, worn or not. So I'll wear it Saturday and send it back Monday. If their policy allows it, there's nothing wrong with doing it.
cue: If their policy allows it, there's nothing wrong with doing it.
explanation: Sofia moves from what the store's policy permits to what's ethically fine. A rule allowing returns tells you what you can get away with, not whether wearing and returning is fair to the store.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Sofia isn't citing custom or how it's always been done; she leaps from a fact about the policy to a moral verdict.

passage: Psychologists have found that people form a first impression of someone within a few seconds of meeting them. Seconds! So stop feeling guilty about judging people fast. If someone gives you a bad vibe in the first ten seconds, you're right to write them off. Trust the first impression.
cue: So stop feeling guilty about judging people fast.
explanation: Derek turns a finding about how people do form impressions into advice about how they should judge others. That snap judgments happen doesn't make them accurate or fair.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Derek doesn't praise snap judgments as natural; he moves from a research finding about what people do to what they ought to do.

title: Re: Starting salary gap
passage: Thanks for raising this, Aaliyah. You're right that new hires who negotiated earn about 7% more than those who took our first offer for the same role, and I'd encourage everyone to negotiate. But that's simply where everyone's pay ended up, and where it ended up is where it should be. I don't see a reason to adjust anyone's pay.
cue: that's simply where everyone's pay ended up, and where it ended up is where it should be
explanation: Bruce treats the gap's existence as its own justification: pay is where it landed, so that's where it should stay. Whether equal work deserves equal pay needs an actual reason, not just a description.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Bruce doesn't appeal to long-standing custom; he goes straight from how pay stands right now to how it should stand.

source: Trustee Marion Feld · Lakeshore school board
passage: The new student laptops are a great investment, and teachers tell me they're already using them well. They also come with software that can log every website a student visits, around the clock. That capability is right there on every machine. So yes, I believe staff should review every student's browsing history each week.
cue: So yes, I believe staff should review every student's browsing history each week
explanation: Marion moves from what the software can do to what staff should do. Being able to monitor every site doesn't settle whether weekly reviews of students' browsing are right.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Nothing here appeals to how things have always been done; the leap is from a technical fact, 'it can log', to a 'should'.

passage:
Seraphine: The cooks asked again this week whether they could get a share of the nightly tips.
Tobiah: Tips get left on the servers' tables, and the servers collect them at the end of every shift.
Tobiah: That's where the money ends up, so that's who it should belong to. The kitchen has its hourly wage.
cue: That's where the money ends up, so that's who it should belong to
explanation: Tobiah goes straight from how tips currently flow, onto the servers' tables, to who should own them. Where the money lands describes the setup; whether the cooks deserve a share needs an actual reason.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Tobiah doesn't claim tips have always gone to servers; he leaps from where the money lands right now to who it ought to belong to.

title: Flickwell defends autoplay, including on kids' profiles
passage: Asked about criticism of autoplay at an industry conference, Flickwell product chief Harold Banks said viewers watch about 40% longer when the next episode starts automatically, including on children's profiles. 'The data tells us what serves our viewers,' he said, adding that keeping autoplay on by default is the right thing to do.
cue: The data tells us what serves our viewers
explanation: Banks treats a fact about viewing time as proof of what's good for viewers. Watching longer shows autoplay holds attention, not that it's right, especially for kids.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Banks never says autoplay is natural; he slides from a measured fact about behavior to a claim about what's right.

title: Afternoon air quality on floor 2
passage: Our new monitors show CO2 on floor 2 above 1,400 ppm most afternoons. Our facilities policy commits us to keeping indoor CO2 under 1,000 ppm, the level we adopted as our ventilation standard. Since we've agreed that's the standard we should meet, we ought to raise the air handler's fresh-air setting, which the vendor says will bring us back under.
cue: Our facilities policy commits us to keeping indoor CO2 under 1,000 ppm
explanation: Aisha's 'ought' doesn't come from the readings alone. She states the value premise openly, the policy's commitment, and then shows the facts fall short of it.

whyNot.fal_is_ought: The step to 'should' is bridged by a stated, agreed standard, so the conclusion isn't drawn from facts alone.

source: Dr. Kenji Watanabe, pediatrician · Halden school board
passage: During puberty, teens' sleep cycles shift later, so many can't fall asleep before 11 p.m. With our 7:20 a.m. start, most of our students get under seven hours a night, well short of what pediatric guidelines recommend. This board has said its schedule should support students' health and learning. Given that commitment, we ought to move the start to 8:30.
cue: This board has said its schedule should support students' health and learning
explanation: Dr. Watanabe pairs facts about teen sleep with a value the board has already endorsed. With that premise stated, the case for a later start follows.

whyNot.fal_is_ought: He doesn't jump from facts straight to 'should'; the board's stated commitment to student health supplies the value premise.
